title: THE OVERLAND GUIDE
subtitle: A Pocket Companion for Emigrants to Oregon, with Necessary Outfits, the Road, and Counsel for the Journey. Independence, 1848.
note: Period voice is authored for the game, after the manner of Joel Palmer's 1847 Journal of Travels (Necessary Outfits for Emigrants, pp. 257-263 of the 1906 reprint) and other guides. Figures in the plain rules are the game's own.

chapters.title: To the Emigrant
chapters.period:
The road to Oregon is long, but it is not a mystery. Hundreds have gone before you, and those who arrived in good order were not the boldest, but the best prepared and the most patient.

Set out from Independence when the grass is up, which is commonly the last of April or the first days of May. Start earlier and your cattle will starve on the bare prairie; start later and the snows of the mountains will meet you before the Cascades. A party that leaves in June must travel hard and waste no days; one that leaves in July had better know what it is about.

Go with a sound wagon, a good team, and provisions for the whole road, and keep some money in your pocket, for the posts beyond the Missouri sell dear.
chapters.plain:
Name five travelers, pick a profession and a departure month, then buy your outfit at the Independence store. Nothing is bought for you: the store starts empty, and the next chapter gives a recommended outfit.

CONTINUE advances the days; PAUSE stops the wagon. Landmarks and encounters stop travel on their own. MAP, GUIDE, HISTORY and PARTY take no time. Hover over any control for a short explanation.

You may also settle short of Oregon at any stop (CAMP > CABIN / SETTLE HERE): Missouri and the Willamette edge are open, a post takes you on unless it refuses you over crimes, and in Native country the people there decide; stay where they refuse and you are run off. Every ending is scored: travelers by health, goods at Independence prices, cash and keepsakes, multiplied by the ending (Oregon 1, settled 0.6, run off 0.3, turned back 0.25, lost 0) and by the banker's purse over yours. The journey to Oregon City is about 1,938 guide miles by Palmer's table. A careful party takes most of a year; the trade-off between time and risk is the heart of the game.
chapters.caption: Independence, Missouri, in the outfitting season.

chapters.title: Of the Outfit
chapters.period:
Every grown person should be provided with two hundred pounds of flour, thirty of pilot bread, seventy-five of bacon, ten of rice and twenty-five of sugar, besides coffee, beans, dried fruit and ten pounds of salt.

The wagon should be light, strong and well seasoned, and should not be loaded above twenty-five hundred pounds. For a team, three yoke of good oxen will serve and a fourth is no waste: oxen are slower than mules, but cheaper, hardier, less apt to be stolen, and good beef at the last. Carry a spare wheel, axle and tongue; a broken one in the mountains may cost a week.

Each man should have a good rifle with powder and lead, and every person stout clothing and boots for the cold. A few simples for sickness are worth their weight. Dried apples or peaches are no luxury: they keep off the scurvy.
chapters.plain:
Palmer's five weighed staples for five grown travelers come to 1,700 lb, the food in the outfit below. The game's cargo limit is 2,500 lb and Independence sells at most 2,000 lb of food, so the wagon fills before your money runs out. Every profession leaves with about the same food; what your purse buys is restocking at the posts once the wagon's food runs low, usually around the fifth month.

Oxen pull in a working team of up to six; extra oxen are spares. Food is counted in food units; a person eats more on fuller rations. Fresh produce spoils in three days; dried fruit keeps for months.
chapters.caption: An outfitter's counter at Independence.

chapters.title: Of Horses and Mules
chapters.period:
Many go out on horseback or with pack mules and leave the wagon at home. A pack train travels faster than oxen and goes where no wagon can, but it carries little, and every pound must be weighed. The mule packs more and stands hardship better; the horse is better under the saddle.

Look to your animals' backs every night and graze them well, for a starved horse is soon a dead one. Guard them always: the Indian and the white thief alike prize a horse above all your other goods. Two may ride one horse to outrun trouble for a day, but no further.
chapters.plain:
The wagon is a store item; leave without one and you set out as packers. Horses $40, mules $50, saddle and bridle $15, pack saddle $5, saddlebags $3. A rider with saddlebags carries 75 lb of freight; a pack saddle, or a led horse, 225 lb; walkers carry packs of up to 50 lb each. Travel > ALLOW HEAVY LOAD raises the limits at the cost of speed and wear, and LEAD ANIMALS frees the riders' weight at walking pace.

With a saddle for everyone the party rides, about 32 miles a day before pace and country; with too few saddles it walks as a pack train. DOUBLE UP puts two to a saddle at riding pace but wears the animals four times as fast: good for a getaway, not for the road. Animals lose condition on carrying days, more in sagebrush, and recover with rest; one ridden to nothing gives out.

Horse thieves come only for parties with animals; a NIGHT GUARD or a watchdog makes them rarer. Ford with the horses in low water and swim them in high. Posts, traders and the Nez Perce at the Grande Ronde trade horses, and a horse or mule can be butchered for meat. Riders escape pursuit more often, but never always.
chapters.caption: Nez Perce horses at the Grande Ronde.

chapters.title: Of the Road
chapters.period:
From Independence the road crosses the Kansas and the Big Blue to the Platte, and follows that broad, shallow river to Fort Laramie. Fort Kearny, newly built on the Platte, is the only army post on the whole road; Laramie and Bridger are trading houses, and Fort Hall, Boise and Walla Walla belong to the Hudson's Bay Company.

At every post the prices rise the farther west you go. Flour that cost two dollars a hundred in Missouri will cost twenty at Fort Hall. Trade at the posts for what you lack, but do not expect to be outfitted there.

Take your time at good grass and water, and make your distance where the road is easy. A party that drives its cattle to death on the Platte will walk the Snake.

Beyond Bridger's a road turns off to the Mormon settlement by the Great Salt Lake. The Saints are short of bread this year and sell little, but they want cloth and cattle. From their valley a new cutoff runs north of the lake to the California road and back to the Snake at the Raft River; it was a pack trail until returning soldiers of the Mormon Battalion opened it to wagons in September.

At the Raft River the Applegates' South Road follows the California road to the Humboldt, then strikes northwest across the Black Rock desert, the Goose Lake and Klamath country, and down the Rogue and Umpqua to the head of the Willamette. It was opened in 1846 to keep emigrants off the Columbia, and it misses the Blue Mountains, the Cayuse country and the Barlow toll. It is some three hundred miles longer. There is no post or trader on it, the drive to Black Rock is long and dry, the natives along it shoot stock from cover, and the Umpqua canyon is a trap when the fall rains come. The first companies over it in 1846 were on the road until December.
chapters.plain:
Each trading visit costs one day and meals, however many trades you make. Post counters have limited stock; passing traders (TALK TO TRADERS) sell fixed lots at higher prices. Sell prices follow the region and are always below what you would pay.

Pace and rations can be changed at any time. A faster pace covers more ground but wears the oxen down faster and tires the travelers: at a strenuous pace a well-fed party no longer mends on the move, and at a grueling pace everyone loses a little health every day; short rations stretch food but raise illness. Rest in camp to recover people and animals.

The Salt Lake road leaves Fort Bridger and rejoins the main road at the Raft River, about a hundred miles longer than the road by Fort Hall. In 1848 wagons cannot take the cutoff north of the lake until September 15; walkers and riders can go at once. The South Road (Applegate) leaves at the Raft River and rejoins at Oregon City: about 990 miles against about 680 by the Columbia, with no traders, a waterless leg to Black Rock, raids on the stock in the Paiute, Pit River, Modoc and Rogue River country (a night guard or a watchdog helps), and snow at Fandango Pass and the Cascade summit in winter. The trail map marks each Native nation along the road and where the road passes from one people's country to another.
chapters.caption: Chimney Rock, on the North Platte.

chapters.title: Of Rivers
chapters.period:
Never cross a river in a hurry. Low water may be forded with care; when the river is up, raise the wagon bed, float it, or pay the ferryman, and think the money well spent. Rain upstream will raise a river while you sit beside it.

At the Green River there is a ferry at the southern crossing. Below The Dalles you may go by the Columbia on rafts, a dangerous passage at the Cascades, or over the mountain by the Barlow road.
chapters.plain:
Fording is free and fastest but risks the wagon, the load and the animals; it is safest when the water is low. Ferries cost money and are free of risk. Walkers and riders wade, swim or let the horses carry them.

At the Cascades you portage around the rapids, often with Native help, or steer the raft through yourself.
chapters.caption: The ferry at the Kansas River.

chapters.title: Of the Camp
chapters.period:
A day in camp is not a day lost. Let the cattle graze, mend the wagon, nurse the sick, and send the best shot out for meat. Give every hand his work and let the tired rest.

If winter catches you where there is timber, build a cabin; a fortnight's work will shelter a family through the cold. And if you would go no farther, many a good farm lies short of the Willamette, but ask the people of the place whether you are welcome.
chapters.plain:
CAMP opens the camp menu; looking costs no time. REST rests 1 to 30 days and stops early for trouble or a food warning. COMPANION TASKS gives each companion a standing job for camp days: rest, forage, dry meat, nurse a patient, help the leader hunt, fish nearby, guard the stock, repair the wagon or work leather. Workers miss their rest. A Carpenter repairs fastest; anyone can patch with a care kit.

FIELD TRIPS sends hunters out on foot for a day or riding for one to three. CARE spends care kits on the sick and hurt. LIVESTOCK picks up to six working oxen and tends cows, goats and hens. CABIN / SETTLE HERE builds a cabin at a stop with timber (a hatchet and about fifteen worker-days) or ends the journey there; see the first chapter for settling.
chapters.caption: A night camp on the prairie.

chapters.title: Of Keeping Food
chapters.period:
Fresh meat will not keep three days in summer. Cut what you cannot eat in thin strips and dry it over a slow fire or in the sun, as the mountain men do; a little salt makes it keep longer and waste less. Dried meat is light and carries well.

Gather greens and berries where they grow, and dry what you cannot eat, for they will keep off the scurvy weeks later. Eat first what will spoil first, and do not throw away good food to lighten the wagon while the cattle can bear it.
chapters.plain:
Fresh meat, fish and produce spoil within days; the party always eats what spoils soonest. Camp > PRESERVE MEAT spends a day drying up to 100 lb of fresh meat. Plain drying keeps 80% of the food value for up to 21 days; salt-assisted drying uses salt (about 5% of the meat's weight) and keeps 90% for up to 30 days. Dried meat weighs about a third as much.

Camp > DRY FRUIT / GREENS dries up to eight baskets in a day; a basket is 4 lb of fresh produce. Dried produce is far lighter and keeps up to 90 days, but gives only a quarter of the vitamin C. Food is counted in food units of about 1,000 calories. RATIONS (Travel) are bare, meager or filling.
chapters.caption: Drying racks at the Dalles.

chapters.title: Of Game and Stock
chapters.period:
Buffalo, antelope and deer will be found along the road, but do not trust your rifle to feed you. A good hunter will keep the camp in fresh meat in the buffalo country and go hungry in the sagebrush. Dry or salt what you cannot eat, for fresh meat will not keep three days in summer.

Your oxen are your life. Graze them well, rest them when they fail, and never overdrive them in heat or on bad water. If one must be killed, it is still beef; and if one dies, do not leave it to the wolves.
chapters.plain:
Hunting takes a day and ammunition; you carry back only what the party can haul. Foraging takes a day and depends on the season, region and healthy gatherers. CAMP > PRESERVE MEAT dries fresh meat, with salt for better keeping.

The team loses condition on working days and recovers on rest days with grass. Worn-out animals slow the wagon. You can slaughter a spare ox (CAMP > LIVESTOCK), and a starved animal can be butchered rather than wasted. Milk cows, goats and hens give food on the road if fed.

Where a river is within reach, Hunt & forage > FISH spends a day casting: strike when the bobber goes under. Milk cows, goats and laying hens can be bought at Independence and the posts; fed and rested, they give milk and eggs on the road.
chapters.caption: Crossing the Big Blue with the cattle.

chapters.title: Of Dogs
chapters.period: A good farm dog is worth his keep. He will wake the camp when strangers come near, turn up game for the hunter, and keep a man company on a long night's watch. But he must eat when there is no game, and the rivers take many a dog that the ferry would have saved.
chapters.plain:
One working dog, $5 at Independence or at a post (Camp > DOG, where you can also name it). Give it a job: CAMP WATCH warns of bandits, riders and horse thieves and makes horse thieves rarer; HELP HUNT goes on the leader's hunts, may find game when the search turns up nothing, catches rabbits, and lets you hunt with no bullets; REST lets it recover.

People eat first; then the dog eats 1.2 food units a day at rest and 1.6 when working or traveling. Choose whether it shares what is left, waits until tomorrow's meals are kept back, or gets nothing. A hungry, tired or weak dog will not work. A river mishap can drown it; a ferry is safe.
chapters.caption: A farm shepherd at the Elm Grove.

chapters.title: Of Sickness
chapters.period:
The Platte is the home of the cholera and the bloody flux. Drink from springs where you can, camp away from old camps, and keep the sick apart and warm.

The scurvy comes on slowly, after long weeks of salt meat and bread. The gums soften, old wounds open, and the strongest man grows weak. Greens, berries and dried fruit drive it off, and a man who has it will mend if he gets them. Fresh game helps a little, but will not cure it alone.
chapters.plain:
Each traveler has their own health and conditions; open PARTY to inspect them. Care kits treat illness and injury, and a Caregiving companion (or a doctor leader) makes care work better.

Vitamin C comes from fresh produce, foraged greens and berries, and dried fruit; freshly killed meat gives a little. Scurvy begins after about six weeks without it. Alone it weakens a traveler down to a floor and then wears them down very slowly; given produce, they recover. Dried fruit is only opened when the party actually needs it.
chapters.caption: A grave beside the road.

chapters.title: Of Winter
chapters.period:
The mountains are no place for a late party. Snow may close South Pass and the Blue Mountains from November, and the Barlow road over Mount Hood is shut to wagons from November until the spring. Barlow's own company was caught there in '45 and had to leave its wagons in the snow.

If winter finds you, do not stop on the climb. The valleys below the passes give some shelter, though little grass. Push over the pass while your cattle can still stand, or winter in a valley and go on in spring.
chapters.plain:
From November to March (April on the Barlow road) the high passes are snow country. On the climb, some days are snowbound with no progress, and animals lose condition every day, even in camp, because there is no grass; worn-out animals can die. Camped in a valley below a pass, there are no snowbound days, but the animals still weaken slowly.

The Barlow road is closed to wagons from November to April; the Columbia, resting, or going on foot remain open. From November to February the Columbia is cold and windy: every day afloat costs some health, wind pins the raft ashore on some days, and a wreck at the Cascades drowns more often. In a hard winter (about one in four) the river freezes in January and February and no raft can launch until March. Wherever there is timber and a hatchet, CAMP > CABIN builds a log cabin at a stop: about fifteen worker-days, every fit and willing traveler working instead of resting, a carpenter half again as fast. A finished cabin keeps out cold exposure and storms and cuts winter sickness; it does nothing for hunger, scurvy or animals without grass. The season notice warns you from September.
chapters.caption: The Barlow road under snow.

chapters.title: Of Trade and Work
chapters.period:
Money is not the only coin on this road. The trader at the post will take skins, a horse or a good coat; an emigrant short of flour will pay well for it, and the Mormons want cloth. A party with a carpenter or a saddler among it can find work at the posts and settlements.

Sell nothing you will want before the next post, and do not expect a fair price for what the trader has no use for.
chapters.plain:
STORE at a post (one day a visit, limited stock, prices rising westward). TALK TO TRADERS for passing traders, who sell fixed lots dearer. VISIT EMIGRANT CAMP to barter with families. Nobody buys for as much as they sell.

Bison, deer and rabbits give trade skins if you carry them back from the hunt; preparing them takes a camp day. FIND WORK at some stops pays wages for days of labor, more for skilled trades. A Leatherworker turns deer hides into buckskin gloves (Camp > LEATHERWORK). A keepsake can be sold with its owner's consent, or carried to Oregon for points.

FIND COMPANIONS hires or takes on travelers where people live. A post can sell you more wagons; each needs a driver and its own oxen (Supplies > Wagons & teams).
chapters.caption: A trader's camp on the road.

chapters.title: Of the Native Peoples
chapters.period:
The native people along the road are not one people but many, each with its own country and its own ways. Most will deal fairly: the Pawnees on the Platte, the Shoshones about Fort Hall, the Nez Perces with their fine horses at the Grande Ronde, and the river people at the Dalles and the Cascades, who know the water better than any white man.

Pay for what you take, and for help when it is given. A wrong done to one family is soon known to its kin.
chapters.plain:
Seven stops have a VISIT action: Pawnee families on the Platte, Northern Shoshone and Bannock families near Fort Hall, Nez Perce horse traders at the Grande Ronde, Umatilla families, Deschutes river families, Wasco families at The Dalles and Upper Chinookan portage crews at the Cascades. Talking is free; buying provisions takes a day.

Households offer provisions, work, barter, horses, a guide, help at a crossing (it lowers the risk), the Cascades portage, and an introduction to a possible companion. Each household remembers how you dealt with it. A crime against one closes its dealings and is answered by its own council (see Of the Law).
chapters.caption: Umatilla families at their gardens.

chapters.title: Of Callings
chapters.period: It matters what a man was before he set out. The farmer knows his cattle, the carpenter his wagon, the hunter his rifle and the doctor his patients; the merchant drives a bargain, and the banker has money, which answers for a great deal. Choose your company with the same care: a willing hand is worth more than a strong one who will not work.
chapters.plain:
Your profession sets your starting purse and gives the leader a skill like a companion's background: merchant (Trading), doctor (Caregiving), carpenter (Carpentry), saddler (Leatherworking), hunter (Hunting, steadier aim), farmer (Stockman: easier on the team, better foraging, butchering and dairy), soldier (Soldiering: a Veteran's service and a soldier's aim) and outlaw (Outlawry: crime experience). The banker has no trade skill, only the largest purse. A leader's skill needs the leader fit to use it.

Companions have their own backgrounds, temperaments and trust. Hired companions expect wages; trust falls with hardship and hard choices, and companions who lose it may leave. If the leader dies, the journey ends.
chapters.caption: Emigrants making ready at Independence.

chapters.title: Of the Law
chapters.period: Beyond the Missouri there is no court but the company you travel with, and the soldiers at Fort Kearny. That is no license. Word travels faster on this road than you would think, and a party that robs or kills will find the posts shut against it and men riding after it.
chapters.plain: Crime is never free. Each act is a chance: witnesses, the venue and staff decide whether you are noticed, and experience makes the act itself go smoother. Word of an act travels the road as a description: where it arrives, people may or may not know your party for the ones who did it (likelier the worse the act, less likely as the news grows old; each place decides once). Those who know you refuse you. Tie kerchiefs over your faces before an act and get away clean, and word describes only a masked outfit, rarely put to you; a slipped mask, people who have traded with you there, or anyone who catches you will still know you. Bare-faced, a name that has reached ordinary folk makes them give in to threats more readily; soldiers, posses and Native households are not cowed. Known crimes raise notoriety: posses, regulators and bounty hunters can follow. Capture leads to custody, a hearing and a sentence; killing can hang the leader. Native households answer to their own councils.
chapters.caption: A county jail in Missouri.

chapters.title: Of Arms
chapters.period:
Each man should carry a good rifle and a knife. A shotgun is better at close quarters, and a pistol is of little use but at arm's length. The revolving pistol of Colonel Colt is a wonder, but there are few of them in Missouri and fewer west of it. A hatchet is wanted for wood as much as for defense.

Keep your powder dry and lead enough for the whole road. It is no use to own five guns and one charge.
chapters.plain:
Every traveler sets out with a rifle and a belt knife. The Independence store sells an extra rifle $15, a shotgun $12, a pistol $6, a hatchet $1.50, a knife $1, and one Colt revolver for $50, which no post sells. Posts sell rifles, shotguns, pistols, knives and hatchets at the region's prices.

Hunting needs bullets and a rifle or shotgun; a pistol is no hunting arm. In a fight each traveler takes one firearm and one blade. VIEW PARTY shows who carries what and lets you hand a piece to a chosen traveler; anyone left on AUTO gets what nobody was given, the scarcer pieces first. The rifle reaches farthest; the shotgun holds two loads and hits hardest up close; the Colt fires five quick, lighter shots and is slow to refill; the pistol is quick, cheap and weak. A hatchet hits hardest and a knife strikes quickest. A cabin needs a hatchet. Travelers taken into custody give up the gun and blade they carry until they go free.
chapters.caption: Rifle, shotgun, pistol, Colt's revolver, knife and hatchet.

chapters.title: Of Fighting
chapters.period: Avoid a fight if you honorably can. Most who meet you on the road want trade, a gift or a little of your flour, not blood, and a present made in good humor is cheaper than a funeral. If you must fight, take cover behind the wagons, keep your rifles loaded, and do not all fire at once; a party that empties every gun in the first volley is at the mercy of the second. Tend the wounded after, for a ball or a broken bone does not heal on the march.
chapters.plain: Choosing to fight always opens the tactical fight. Cover blocks shots, reloading costs action points, and wounds and broken bones carry over afterward. Retreating costs what fleeing would. Soldiers and hunters aim better; veterans and won fights steady a traveler's death save.
chapters.caption: Riders stopping a wagon on the road.

outfit_note: Palmer's five weighed staples for five adults (200 flour, 30 pilot bread, 75 bacon, 10 rice, 25 sugar each) total 1,700 lb. He advised four yoke; the game's working team is up to six oxen, so three yoke are listed.
